newsitem.title: UK: UK PSBR forecasts require heavy spending cuts-IFS.
newsitem.headline: UK PSBR forecasts require heavy spending cuts-IFS.

text.p: The forecasts for public sector debt laid out by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown in his first budget will only be met through swingeing spending cuts, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said on Thursday.
In its post-budget briefing, the IFS said the fall forecast for Britain's public sector borrowing requirement incorporates greater revenue from taxes. But the main burden falls on public spending.
Spending will have to fall to 38 percent of national income in 2001/2002, from 41 percent last year.
"These spending cuts cannot conceivably by achieved without a fundamental reappraisal of the role of the state," said John Hall of the IFS.
Brown confirmed in his first budget speech that he would match the spending plans pencilled in by his predecessor, Kenneth Clarke, for two years. "Those plans were always very tight," Hall said.

The PSBR is forecast to drop to 13.3 billion this year, then to 5.4 billion in 1998/99, from 22.7 billion stg last year. Early next century, a hefty public sector surplus is pencilled in to government figures.
All that also assumes that economic growth keeps chugging along steadily, said Andrew Dilnot, director of the IFS. "It assumes the economic cycle is dead. That would be nice, but...." he said.
Whether the public debt targets are met or not, the squeeze is on for the public sector.
"To achieve this, we are talking about reductions in spending in real terms over the planning horizon -- about four billion pounds by the end of the century," Hall said.
To make matters worse, the government's GDP deflator is factoring in increases in inflation over the period, he said. "That will mean resources are even more thinly stretched."
